whyThisMatters: Real security decisions are quick and the wrong option often sounds reasonable. Several bubbles here are habits people genuinely defend, such as one strong password everywhere or approving a prompt to make it stop. This game trains the reflex to judge the habit, not the label.
rememberThis: Sounding secure is not the same as being secure. Ask three quick questions: Is it unique per account? Did I start this request myself? Am I verifying through a channel the sender does not control? If any answer is no, slow down.

discussionPrompts: Ask which bubble people almost tapped wrongly. 'Reuse one strong password everywhere' is a favourite: one breach elsewhere lets attackers replay that password on other sites (credential stuffing).

Ask why approving an MFA prompt you did not start is bad even though MFA is good. The attacker already has the password and is hoping for fatigue; an unexpected prompt means the password is compromised and should be reported and changed.
Ask why SMS codes still count as good while a short password with symbols does not. Which attack does each stop, and which does it not?
Ask why 'Click Unsubscribe' in unknown spam is risky. It confirms your address is live and the link can lead to a tracking or fake page.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like security, or avoiding anything that sounds like a hassle, without asking what the habit really protects against. The 6 trick bubbles plus borderline habits such as Unsubscribe in spam, MFA prompts and cafe Wi-Fi banking catch that reflex.

bubbles.text: Turn on MFA for email and banking
bubbles.why: A stolen password alone can't open your account when MFA is on.

bubbles.text: Check the full sender address
bubbles.why: Fake senders often hide behind a familiar name but have a different address.

bubbles.text: Forward phish to security as attachment
bubbles.why: Sending it as an attachment gives security the details needed to block it.

bubbles.text: Keep an offline, tested backup
bubbles.why: A tested offline backup lets you recover if ransomware locks your files.

bubbles.text: Install updates within days of release
bubbles.why: Updates fix security holes that criminals actively use to break in.

bubbles.text: Use a password manager, unique passwords
bubbles.why: Unique passwords mean one leaked password can't unlock your other accounts.

bubbles.text: Lock your screen every time you leave
bubbles.why: A locked screen stops anyone passing by from using your account or data.

bubbles.text: Use company VPN on cafe Wi-Fi
bubbles.why: A VPN stops others on public Wi-Fi from spying on what you send.

bubbles.text: Call back on a number you already have
bubbles.why: A number you already have reaches the real person, not an impostor.

bubbles.text: Hover to see a link's real address
bubbles.why: Hovering reveals if a link really goes where it claims before you click.

bubbles.text: Phone-verify any bank detail change
bubbles.why: A phone check exposes fake bank-change requests before money is sent.

bubbles.text: Reuse one strong password everywhere
bubbles.why: One leaked password would then open every account that uses it.

bubbles.text: Click Unsubscribe in unknown spam
bubbles.why: Unsubscribe links in spam confirm your address is live and can lead to malware.

bubbles.text: Approve an MFA prompt you did not start
bubbles.why: An unexpected prompt means an attacker has your password and wants your approval.

bubbles.text: Pause antivirus to run a tool faster
bubbles.why: Pausing antivirus lets malware run unchecked while protection is off.

bubbles.text: Share your login to get cover
bubbles.why: Shared logins hide who did what and let anyone with the password in.

bubbles.text: Postpone updates for months
bubbles.why: Delayed updates leave known security holes open for attackers to use.

bubbles.text: Cafe Wi-Fi, then banking without VPN
bubbles.why: Others on public Wi-Fi may be able to spy on your banking details.

bubbles.text: Use a free cracked licence key
bubbles.why: Cracked software often comes with hidden malware that steals data.

bubbles.text: Leave laptop unlocked for a quick coffee
bubbles.why: An unlocked laptop gives anyone nearby instant access to your account.

bubbles.text: Enable macros to view an invoice
bubbles.why: Enabling macros can run hidden malware that infects your computer.

bubbles.text: Delay MFA setup because it is a hassle
bubbles.why: Without MFA, a stolen password is all an attacker needs to get in.

bubbles.text: Never share a code texted to you
bubbles.why: Codes sent to your phone are a lock key; sharing one lets attackers in.

bubbles.text: Use a long passphrase
bubbles.why: Length makes a password hard to guess, even without symbols.

bubbles.text: Use a short password with symbols
bubbles.why: A short password is quick for computers to guess, even with symbols.

bubbles.text: Use a public charging cable
bubbles.why: Public cables or ports can be rigged to install malware or steal data.

bubbles.text: Obey an urgent leader's request
bubbles.why: Criminals pose as leaders and add urgency so you skip the checks.

bubbles.text: Rely on old, unupdated antivirus
bubbles.why: Out-of-date protection misses new threats, so it gives false comfort.
